Improved valorization of sewage sludge in the circular economy by 
anaerobic digestion: Impact of an innovative pretreatment technology 
Nalok Dutta a,1, Anthony T. Giduthuri a,c,1, Muhammand Usman Khan a,e, Richard Garrison b, 
Birgitte K. Ahring a,c,d,* 
a Bioproducts, Sciences and Engineering Laboratory, Washington State University, Tri-Cities, Richland, WA 99354, United States 
b Clean-Vantage LLC, 99354 Richland, WA, United States 
c The Gene and Linda Voiland School of Chemical Engineering and Bioengineering, Washington State University, Pullman, WA 99163, United States 
d Department of Biological Systems Engineering, Washington State University, Pullman, WA 99163, United States 
e Department of Energy Systems Engineering, University of Agriculture, Faisalabad, Pakistan   
A R T I C L E  I N F O   
Keywords: 
Enhanced anaerobic digestion 
Sewage sludge pretreatment 
Advanced wet-oxidation and steam explosion 
Thermophilic anaerobic digestion 
Optimization of pretreatment 
A B S T R A C T   
Anaerobic digestion (AD) of sewage sludge shows low carbon conversion efficiency (CCE) due to the poor 
biodegradability of sewage sludge. The lack of digestibility is specifically linked to the waste-activated sludge 
(WAS) making up the majority of sewage sludge along with a smaller portion of primary sludge, depending on 
the wastewater treatment plant configuration. In this study, we examine the Advanced Wet Oxidation & Steam 
Explosion process (AWOEx) for improving the CCE of digested sewage sludge (DSS) by thermophilic AD. The 
effect of the pretreatment temperature in the range between 160 and 185 ◦C at a fixed residence time of 20 min 
with and without oxygen added at a dosage of 5 % of the organics present was tested. Methane yield improved by 
97.92 % to 183.91 ± 4.93 mL/g vS over the untreated DSS (control), whose methane yield was 92.92 ± 9.07 
mL/g vS We have demonstrated for the first time that 84 % of the organics in sewage sludge can successfully be 
transformed into biogas following AWOEx pretreatment, which can contribute significantly to the circular 
economy instead of greenhouse gas emissions from landfilling.   
1. 1.Introduction 
More than 13.84 million US dry tons (12.56 million metric dry tons) 
of sewage is produced annually in the US from publicly owned treatment 
works or wastewater treatment facilities (WWTF) (Seiple et al., 2017; 
Venkatesan et al., 2015). Sewage sludge, also referred as biosolids, by 
the U.S. Environmental protection Agency (U.S. EPA) is a byproduct 
from the WWTFs that needs disposal. Also, it should be noted that sludge 
management may demand a significant share of the WWTF’s overall 
energy requirement (Capodaglio & Olsson, 2020). Though several 
technologies are being developed for valorizing sewage sludge, imple­
menting these solutions at small-scale communities is still a challenge 
due to unfavorable economics. However, of late, under various param­
eter variables (season, temperature, and ambient humidity), a 
completely solar-powered greenhouse facility for sewage sludge drying 
was examined, and potential improvements for its efficiency were 
assessed (Boguniewicz-Zablocka et al., 2021). Due to its high organic 
content, digested sewage sludge (DSS) can be used to produce bioenergy 
and biofuels. Around 50 % of the US’s WWTFs, corresponding to 7,500 
total WWTFs, convert their sewage sludge to biogas, a mixture of 
methane (ca. 60 %) and carbon dioxide (ca. 40 %) using anaerobic 
digestion (AD). Analyses have shown that the digestate produced after 
AD contains a large portion of organics, which needs further processing 
before conversion to valuable bioenergy or bio-products (Li et al., 2017; 
Nordell et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2020). Several thermal pretreatment 
technologies have been developed for enhancing AD of DSS (Cambi THP, 
Veolia Exelys) (Abu-Orf & Goss, 2012; Bora et al., 2020). However, these 
methods are tailored for upfront pretreatment of the sewage sludge and 
not on specific treatment of the recalcitrant fraction of sewage sludge. 
Also, these technologies use far less severe operational conditions 
(temperatures of ca. 160 ◦C), and the biogas yields are generally only 
improved by ca. 30 %. (Nguyen et al., 2021; Seiple et al., 2020; Wang 
et al., 2021; Yan et al., 2022). Methane yields from the conventional AD 
of sewage sludge have been reported to range between 0.19 and 0.24

Nm3/kg VSin (Di Capua et al., 2020) and the residual organics are 
generally concentrated and disposed of in landfills, on agricultural land 
and parks, or by incineration (Nguyen et al., 2021). However, some 
thermochemical processes like pyrolysis can recover nutrients from 
digestate by converting the residual organics into energy rich gas 
streams, promoting circular economy. Though this is more sustainable 
than incineration, it require further processing to close the carbon loop 
(Callegari & Capodaglio, 2018). 
To overcome these shortcomings, we implemented Advanced Wet 
Oxidation and Steam Explosion (AWOEx) (a thermochemical procedure 
integrating wet oxidation and steam explosion) (Ahring & Munck, 2013; 
Miklos et al., 2018; Svensson et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2020) followed by a 
secondary AD (AD2). 
In the current pretreatment process i.e., AWOEx, biomass materials 
are subjected to oxidizing agents such as air, hydrogen peroxide, or 
oxygen under high temperatures (over 160◦Celsius) and high pressures 
(over 10 bars) for 15 to 45 min (Ahring & Munck, 2013; Biswas et al., 
2015; Biswas et al., 2020; M’Arimi et al., 2020). The AWOEx process 
significantly enhances the solubilization of lignin and hemicellulose in 
lignocellulosic biomass including the crystalline cellulose that is 
retained in the solid fraction (Biswas et al., 2020; Khan & Ahring, 2020). 
As a result of the AWOEx pretreatment, microbial cell wall is disrupted 
and complex structures are broken down. As a result the digestibility of 
the sludge improves resulting in better degradation and disruption of 
both extracellular and intracellular organic matter during the hydrolysis 
step of AD. Thus after pretreatment, hydrolytic enzymes of the microbial 
population will be more effective leading to an increased methane yield 
(Pilli et al., 2020; Sudalyandi & Jeyakumar, 2022; Yadav et al., 2022). 
Additionally, acetic acid formed via de-esterification of the acetyl 
groups, affects the hemicellulosic dissolution into the aqueous solution 
(Biswas et al., 2020; Biswas et al., 2014). The AWOEx pretreatment also 
has several advantages besides its effectiveness, such as requiring no 
chemicals to be recovered, along with a lower formation of inhibitory 
by-products. It is possible to perform AWOEx pretreatment at dry matter 
concentrations up to 45 %, lowering the cost of the pretreatment (Biswas 
et al., 2020). Despite extensive testing of AWOEx on various lignocel­
lulosic biomass materials, the process has not been previously studied 
with sewage sludge as the raw material. In the current study, DSS that 
has already been digested using conventional single-staged AD before 
dewatering and the solids have been pretreated using the AWOEx pre­
treatment method. The pretreated sludge is then fed into a second AD 
step, resulting in a two-staged AD. This process provides a way to make 
the recalcitrant fraction of the sludge available for digestion. 
Many researchers have investigated recycling and reuse of sludge 
from WWTPs as a viable sustainable choice since there is an increased 
focus on mitigating the potential negative effect of land applying sewage 
sludge as well as the need for reducing landfilling of wet organic waste 
materials (Gupta et al., 2021; Smol et al., 2015). In the circular economy 
perspective, the prime focus is on re-use of the waste as a raw material, 
which not only avoids the costs associated with waste disposal but 
instead valorizes the waste as the products and byproducts trickle into 
the economy. Therefore, sludge reuse with a focus on energy recovery is 
a prominent waste management option and a cornerstone of circular 
economy for WWTP (Eliche-Quesada et al., 2011). In this study, we 
determined the effect of AWOEx pretreatment on DSS and optimized the 
pretreatment temperature for sustained high methane yield by ther­
mophilic AD. To understand the impact of AWOEx on the specific 
components of the DSS, we performed composition analysis of the DSS 
out of the secondary AD (AD2). 
2. Materials and methods 
2.1. Advanced wet oxidation & steam explosion pretreatment 
DSS was collected from the Walla Walla WWTP in Eastern Wash­
ington and then dewatered using a filter press before pretreatment. All 
samples of DSS before and after pretreatment were stored at 4 ◦C before 
use. 
The AWOEx pretreatment of DSS was carried out in a 100 L stainless 
steel pressure tank. In each run, 10 kg of dewatered DSS with initial total 
solids conc of ca. 11 wt% was fed into the reactor at a constant mixing 
speed of 50 rpm. The target temperature was achieved by steam addition 
into the pretreatment reactor while the temperature was kept constant 
using an external jacketed oil heater. Oxygen (O2) was purged into the 
reactor based on the amount of vS of DSS while increasing the mixing 
speed to 85 rpm. At the end of residence time, the material was flashed 
out of the tank into a 250 L flash tank. After cooling, the sample was 
collected and stored at 4 ◦C for future experiments and analysis. 
2.2. Design of experiments and statistical analysis 
The Advanced Wet Oxidation & Steam Explosion (AWOEx) pre­
treatment of DSS was performed at temperatures ranging from 160 
to185◦C, without and with oxygen (5 % of the VS) at a residence time of 
20 min. Using the design of experiments (DOE) module (JMP Pro 15.2.0 
- SAS Institute Inc. Cary, NC, USA), 12 experiment conditions at tem­
peratures from 160 ◦C to 185 ◦C with 5 ◦C interval, without and with 
oxygen added (5 % of the VS) and a control without any pretreatment 
(Table 1) are defined based on the full factorial design for combined 
testing of the following categorical factors: temperature (6 level – 
160 ◦C, 165 ◦C, 170 ◦C, 175 ◦C, 180 ◦C, 185 ◦C) and effect of oxygen 
addition (2 level – without oxygen and with oxygen at 5 % of VS) by 
recording the biogas produced for each condition. 
2.3. Anaerobic digestion of pretreated DSS 
Anaerobic digestion (AD) of DSS was conducted in a series of 1 L 
bioreactors (in duplicates) operated in semi-continuous mode with a 
working volume of 400 mL and with a water displacement setup to re­
cord the biogas volume produced from each reactor. The initial inoc­
ulum used was the raw sludge procured from the Walla Walla WWTP 
and digested sludge from the same plant mixed at a ratio of 1:1. The vS 
loading was always maintained at 70 wt% of the TS. The hydraulic 
retention time (HRT) was kept constant at 16 days throughout the ex­
periments, and all bioreactors were fed every 48 h with a recording of 
the biogas produced. One bioreactor was set as control and was fed with 
DSS without pretreatment. All the experiments were run at thermophilic 
conditions (55 ◦C) for total of three retention cycles (48 days). Upon 
stable experimental data, particularly volume and composition of 
biogas, AD experiments were considered complete at the end of the 
stable retention cycle. The methane yield data collected from the ex­
periments was analyzed using two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) 
test (JMP Pro 15.2.0, SAS Institute Inc. Cary, NC, USA) to determine the 
effect of pretreatment conditions and its significance on improving the

2.4. Composition analysis 
The moisture contents (MC), total solids (TS), volatile solids (VS), 
carbohydrates (cellulose and hemicellulose), lignin, and lipid content of 
all samples before and after AWOEx of DSS, DSS and AD were measured 
following the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) methods 
as previously described studies (Biswas et al., 2020; Hames et al., 2008; 
Van Wychen et al., 2016). Protein contents of all samples before and 
after AWOEx of DSS and DSS were measured by the Lowry method 
(Amin et al., 2021; Gonz´alez L´opez et al., 2010). NREL standard method 
was used for determining total lignin (acid-soluble and acid-insoluble) 
and total cellulose and hemicellulose (Sluiter et al., 2008). Acid solu­
ble lignin was determined using a UV spectrophotometer at 205 nm 
(Korpinen et al., 2014), whereas total carbohydrates (sum of glucose, 
xylose, and arabinose) were determined after two-step acid hydrolysis 
(Jenway 6405 UV/Visible, NJ, USA) at a wavelength of 320 nm (Biswas 
et al., 2020; Khan & Ahring, 2020). Monomers were analyzed by using 
an UltiMate® 3000 HPLC system (Dionex, Sunnyvale, CA) with the 
Aminex® 87H Column 250 × 4.6 mm (Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA) with a 
Shodex RI-101 refractive index detector at 60 ◦C using 4 mM sulfuric 
acid as an eluent at a flow rate of 0.6 mL/min. All measurements of 
lignin and carbohydrates analysis were done in duplicates. The lipid 
extraction was performed following chloroform–methanol extraction 
method proposed by Bligh and Dyer (Bligh & Dyer, 1959). 1 g of dried 
sludge was mixed with 20 mL of mixed liquor (chloroform: methanol =
2:1, v/v) and then subjected to 60 ◦C for 4 h. Thereafter, the mixture was 
placed in a centrifuge for 15 min at 3000 rpm and the solvent phase was 
transferred to a glass vial. After evaporating the solvent at 60◦C, the vial 
was weighed. The difference in weight was the total lipid content. 
2.5. Volatile fatty acids analysis 
The concentration of volatile fatty acids was determined in the 
influent and effluent samples for each bioreactor at the start and end of 
every retention cycle using high performance liquid chromatography 
(HPLC) as previously described (Khan & Ahring, 2020). 2 mL of each 
sample was taken and centrifuged at 10, 000 RPM for 10 min. The su­
pernatant was separated with pipette, diluted 2 times with MiliQ water 
and then filtered through 0.2 µm syringe filter. The samples were 
analyzed by UltiMate® 3000 HPLC system (Dionex, Sunnyvale, CA) with 
an Aminex® 87H column 250 × 4.6 mm (Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA) with a 
Shodex RI-101 refractive index detector using 4 mM sulfuric acid as 
eluent.

3. Results and discussion 
3.1. Effect of the AWOEx pretreatment on DSS 
The characteristics of DSS are shown in Table 2. DSS contained 
86.44 % of moisture contents (MS), 13.56 % of total solids (TS), and 
5.78 % of volatile solids (VS) which is 77.8 % of TS. The results were 
similar to previously reported data (Nordell et al., 2021; Usman et al., 
2019). Further, it was found that DSS contained 2.3 % cellulose, 2.9 % 
hemicellulose, 0.9 % lignin, 1.69 % of crude fat and 3.01 % of protein. 
Based on the statistical analysis of the experimental data for both the 
tested categorical variables, addition of oxygen significantly improved 
methane yield for all the temperatures ranges of the pretreatment (p <
0.0003). On the other hand, temperature improved methane yield (p <
0.057)- but not to an extent as seen in case of oxygen addition. 
We calculated the Cohen’s D to find the implication of the effect size 
on our study. If two groups are the same size and have equal standard 
deviations, Cohen’s d is the suitable effect size measurement. If each 
group has a distinct standard deviation, an alternative metric is Glass’s 
delta, which only considers the standard deviation of the control group. 
An option when there are diverse sample sizes is Hedges’ g, which offers 
a measure of effect size weighted in accordance with the relative size of 
each sample. In our study, Cohen’s d was calculated to be 4.22; Glass’s 
delta was calculated to be 4.41 and Hedges’ g was 4.23. 
3.1.1. Effect of the AWOEx pretreatment on methane yield from DSS 
At the end of HRT 3, the average biogas aaition of methane and 
carbon dioxide were in the range of 62 ± 1.5 vol% and 38 ± 2.2 vol%^, 
respectively, with traces of moisture, hydrogen and oxygen. For the 
control (DSS without pretreatment), methane and carbon dioxide con­
tent were in the range of 55–58 vol% and 40–42 % Fig. 1 shows the 
methane yield from AWOEx pretreated DSS material at temperatures 
ranging from 160 ◦C −
185 ◦C with 20 min residence time and without 
oxygen. Fig. 2 shows the trend in average methane yields from the semi- 
continuous bioreactors at 55 ◦C fed with DSS pretreated at temperatures 
ranging from 160 ◦C to 185 ◦C with 20 min residence time and 5 % 
oxygen. The control reactors were fed with DSS without AWOEx pre­
treatment to compare the effect of the different conditions during 
AWOEx pretreatment on methane production. It was found that the 
average methane yield of the control reactors was 92.92 mL/gVS. The 
average methane yields from 175 ◦C and 170 ◦C were 183.91 and 
170.93 mL/g vS respectively. Since the residence time and oxygen 
dosage were kept constant for the optimally performing sets, it can be 
concluded that the resulting methane yield was solely a function of 
pretreatment temperature. 
The average methane yield at 175 ◦C was higher than 180 ◦C, 170 ◦C 
and 165 ◦C by 18.72 %, 7.59 %, and 23.77 %, respectively. One of the 
possible reasons of lower methane yield at 180 ◦C might be due to the 
formation of inhibitory compounds at higher temperatures as previously

described during the pretreatment of sewage sludge (Hii et al., 2014; 
Su´arez-Iglesias et al., 2017). The highest average methane yields of 
183.92 mL/gvS at 175 ◦C and 170.93 mL/gvS at 170 ◦C was for the same 
residence time and O2 dosage but at different temperatures, indicating 
that lower temperatures might have resulted in a lower hydrolysis of the 
material than higher temperatures. The results for the control reactor 
are in accordance with the study by Nordell et al., 2021, which found 
that only 46 mL/g vS of methane yield was achieved during anaerobic 
digestion of digested sewage sludge under thermophilic condition 
without any thermochemical pretreatment. Overall, AWOEx pretreat­
ment of DSS significantly increased the methane yield far over the 
control reactor based on the ANOVA test (P = 0.0007). Table 3 shows 
the difference of TS and vS % of all bioreactors for the feed and the 
effluent, and it was found that the bioreactors with the highest methane 
yield, 175 ◦C, had the highest TS conversion of 72.82 % out of all the 
groups. Highest single day average methane yield was 191.4 mL/g vS 
and 181.3 mL/g vS observed at the pretreatment temperature of 175 ◦C 
and 180 ◦C, respectively, followed by 180.8 mL/g vS at 170 ◦C. 
Based on our results, optimal temperature range for pretreating DSS 
will be in the range of 170–180 ◦C with oxygen addition. Fig. 3 shows 
the mean methane yield plotted for every pretreatment condition where 
oxygen addition resulted in an increase of the methane yield by 92.65 % 
over the pretreatment groups without oxygen addition at 175 ◦C, the 
temperature with the maximum average methane yield. The increasing 
trend of methane yield with an increase in temperature for 160 to 175 ◦C 
and decreasing trend from 175 to 185 ◦C, further supports that 175 ◦C is 
the optimal temperature for pretreating DSS. 
3.2. Influence of the different operational conditions of AWOEx 
pretreatment of DSS on methane yield 
Oxygen addition had significant (P = 0.0003) and higher effect on 
methane yield next to the temperature (P = 0.0573) as seen in Fig. 3. 
This is in accordance with a previous study on AWOEX pretreatment of 
sawdust (Biswas et al., 2020; Higgins et al., 2017). A previous study 
reported that AWOEx pretreatment increased the formation of small 
molecular weight organics, which is easily biodegradable during AD (Hii 
et al., 2014; Su´arez-Iglesias et al., 2017). Further, the radicals produced 
during AWOEx pretreatment are powerful in oxidizing recalcitrant 
compounds such as lignin, which increased the biodegradability of DSS

molecules into shorter chains (Abelleira-Pereira et al., 2015; Hii et al., 
2014; Liang et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2022; M’Arimi et al., 2020; Su´arez- 
Iglesias et al., 2017). Furthermore, higher O2 pressure during pretreat­
ment rapidly depolymerizes crosslinked bonds of complex compounds 
into simpler chain. The breakdown of bonds is somewhat constrained in 
the absence of oxygen. According to our findings, high temperatures 
enhance the dissolution of DSS, and adding O2 helps in oxidizing organic 
compounds in DSS into digestible molecules. 
3.3. Composition analysis of DSS before and after AWOEx pretreatment- 
AD 
AWOEx treatment affected the composition of DSS significantly. At 
the optimal pretreatment temperature of 175 ◦C, the conversion of 
cellulose was 74.4 %, hemicellulose was 66.8 %, and lignin was 68.8 % 
of the material. However, for the control set (dewatered DSS) only 28.6 
% of the cellulose, 51.2 % of the hemicellulose and 47.2 % of the lignin 
was converted during secondary thermophilic AD. Table 4 shows the 
composition analysis of the influent and effluent of the bioreactors be­
tween 160 and 185 ◦C compared to the control bioreactor. 
The average protein content decreased with 17.3 % and 28.1 % in the 
bioreactors at 175 ◦C and 180 ◦C, respectively, compared to 11.3 % 
protein conversion in the control reactor Thermal hydrolysis do not only 
lead to conversion of lipids, proteins and polysaccharides but simulta­
neously brings about hydrolysis of these compounds into lower molec­
ular weight compounds by cleaving the peptide, ester and glycosidic 
bonds. The crude fat content in the effluent of our bioreactors fed with 
material pretreated at175◦C and 180 ◦C decreased by 78.66 % and 
72.36 %, respectively, compared to 36.15 % reduction in the control 
bioreactor set. In the effluent sets of the bioreactors 175 ◦C and 180 ◦C 
without oxygen, the reduction in crude fat content was 42.85 % and 
41.33 % showing that oxygen triggers an aggressive breakdown of crude 
fats in DSS. This result indicate that highly unsaturated fatty acids are 
more susceptible to oxidative reactions. Polymers in the material need to 
be hydrolyzed in order to allow for methane production by anaerobic 
digestion. Grease and fat hydrolysis into long chain fatty acids, which 
can be further degraded by AD possess a large biogas potential of 
importance for the methane yield. (Wett et al., 2006). 
A recent study reported a hydrolysis of ca. 30 % of the total proteins 
and 25 % of the total polysaccharide content into simpler, smaller or­
ganics following thermic pretreatment (Yang et al., 2019). When ther­
mal hydrolysis temperatures were increased from 120 to 170 ◦C, (Chen 
et al., 2019) reported a 15 % increase in amino acid hydrolysis as 
compared to a 9.7 % increase in proteins hydrolyzed to VFA. Another 
study reported a 60 % increase in the amount of VFA produced from 
protein hydrolysis when the temperature was increased from 160 to 
200 ◦C(Wilson & Novak, 2009). Another study reported that during 
thermal hydrolysis at 160 ◦C for 50 min, around 12 % of particulate 
protein was transformed into VFA (Han et al., 2017). It has been esti­
mated that 13 to 23 % of the total VFA generated in wastewater sludge 
may be generated from the hydrolysis of protein (Wilson & Novak, 
2009). 
Studies also indicate that lipid hydrolysis at ca. 170 ◦C primarily 
contained fractions of aldehydes(80 %) and alcohol(11 %) (Wilson & 
Novak, 2009). During thermal hydrolysis, long-chain fatty acids (LCFA) 
increase in concentration, inhibiting bacteria and methanogens, 
although the inhibitory concentration depends on the LCFA composition 
and microbial species composition. In contrast to saturated fatty acids, 
unsaturated LCFAs were more inhibitive to methanogens at threshold 
concentrations of 10 to 30 mg/L (Lalman & Bagley, 2000). 
The presence of lipids and proteins in wastewater sludge may 
generate compounds which are inhibitory to methanogenesis such as 
ammonia (Liu & Sung, 2002; Tanaka et al., 1997) and hydrophobic fatty

previous study also reported that AWOEX pretreatment showed 
enhanced solubilization of carbohydrates after AWOEx pretreatment, 
which resulted in a higher methane yield during AD of pretreated 
manure fibers (Khan & Ahring, 2020). In this study, we further saw 
improved conversion of other components such as proteins and lipids. As 
a result of the hydrolysis reaction of acetyl groups in hemicellulose 
producing acetic acid, the pretreated DSS after AWOEx at 175 ◦C con­
tained higher concentrations of VFAs (1650 mg/L) (J¨onsson & Martín, 
2016). Acetic acid dominated the organic acids in all bioreactors, and 
the bioreactor that contained the highest concentration of VFA also 
contained the highest concentration of acetic acid (900 mg/L) (Table 5). 
The concentration of VFA in the effluents of all bioreactors were, how­
ever, low (<20 mg/L), indicating that all bioreactors are functioning 
well and all digestible materials are being fully converted to methane. 
One of the major findings of our study was the degradation of crude 
fat and protein in the optimally performing set of reactors at 175 ◦C by 
ca.80 % and 20 %, respectively. It is obvious that this increased con­
version is a major reason for the higher methane yield found after 
AWOEx. Overall, our results show that AWOEx pretreatment of DSS 
results in significant higher methane production compared to standard 
one-step AD of sewage sludge. This higher energy recovery is of major 
importance for valorizing sewage sludge at WWTPs. The study further 
demonstrated that both elevated temperature and oxygen are important 
for improving the carbon conversion of sewage sludge into methane. 
Compared to conventional AD with ca. 50 % vS conversion, incorpo­
rating a secondary AWOEx pretreatment process resulted in 41 % extra 
conversion of organics in sewage sludge with over 100 % net improved 
methane production. This far higher methane production as well as the 
lower residual amount residing needing final disposal could potentially 
be game-changing for exploitation of the energy potential of sewage 
sludge in the future. 
4. Conclusions 
This study demonstrates the efficiency of AWOEx for enhancing 
methane yield of AD of DSS demonstrating a 2-fold increase in methane 
yield compared to untreated DSS far higher than previously reported in 
other studies. The optimal pretreatment condition was found to be a 
temperature of 175 ◦C with oxygen (5 % of VS) added resulting in a 
methane yield of 183.91 ± 4.93 mL/g vS of previous digested sewage 
sludge. Oxygen addition was the most critical parameter in improving 
the methane yield, followed by temperature. Pretreatment with a sec­
ondary AD step in tandem improved the CCE significantly leaving only 
small amounts of organics (15 % of the input VS) behind. From this 
study we also demonstrated that AWOEx not only had a major effect on 
the digestibility of lignocellulosic polymers such as carbohydrates, 
which was present in low amounts in the DSS but also on the lipids and 
protein fraction, which was present in large concentrations in the 
sewage sludge.
